impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims reciting a genus of antibodies (anti-CGRP antagonist humanized monoclonal antibodies) for treating headache, where every member of the claimed genus would be effective for the recited treatment but identifying members of the genus requires undue experimentation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of its panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment claims covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for headache treatment. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines Amgen v. Sanofi enablement principles by sustaining overly broad claims where the difficulty lies in identifying qualifying antibodies rather than demonstrating therapeutic efficacy. The decision preserves the panel's distinction between enablement for method claims versus composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad biologic method-of-treatment claims benefit from the panel's approach, which may allow genus claims to survive enablement challenges when any member of the genus would be therapeutically effective, potentially strengthening protection for pioneering biologic therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face broader blocking patents on biologic methods of treatment, potentially increasing licensing costs and delaying biosimilar or competing biologic development. The dissent signals continued uncertainty and possible future reversal.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results and specifies testing conditions inconsistent with the referenced standard protocol.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that claims of the '287 patent directed to a waterproof breathable membrane were invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured using different methods (upright vs. inverted cup) yielding different results, and the specification's stated test conditions (40°C, 20% RH) conflicted with the referenced ASTM E96-94 standard. The court found a person of ordinary skill could not determine with reasonable certainty whether a product fell within the claimed MVTR range.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and textile technology can challenge patents with performance-metric claims where the specification fails to specify a single, consistent measurement methodology, reducing exposure to infringement liability for ambiguous claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming products by functional performance ranges must ensure their specifications unambiguously identify a single test method and consistent conditions, or risk invalidation. This raises the drafting burden for patents in industries relying on standardized testing protocols.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to constitute a virtual assignment, allowing the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift from active commercialization to patent enforcement did not constitute a cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the license agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarification that enforcement-focused business models do not automatically terminate license agreements and that exclusive licenses conveying all substantial rights allow suit without joining the patent owner, reducing procedural barriers to enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential standing defense, and universities and other patent owners who license exclusively may find it harder to control enforcement activities or argue that licensees have abandoned their rights by shifting to enforcement-only operations.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the trade secret plaintiff's damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding of trade secret misappropriation liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, holding the district court improperly excluded Versata's damages expert testimony and should consider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract damages award and reinstated it, while affirming the jury's finding that Ford misappropriated Versata's trade secrets in developing competing automotive configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the court's instruction that district courts must give fair consideration to multiple damages methodologies and cannot lightly override jury damages findings on breach of contract claims, potentially increasing recoveries in software misappropriation cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face continued trade secret misappropriation exposure. The remand for a new damages trial with expanded expert testimony could result in significantly larger damage awards against Ford and similarly situated defendants.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility under § 101 for claims related to non-uniform constellation designs used in broadcast communications. The court vacated the eligibility finding for certain claims of two patents while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents, affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings including willfulness, and remanded for further proceedings on the vacated claims. The case involved LG televisions implementing the ATSC 3.0 broadcast standard.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for some claims and the sustained jury verdict on infringement and damages, reinforcing that standard-essential patents with concrete technical improvements can survive § 101 challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face ongoing patent infringement risk and substantial damages exposure. The partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about which claim formulations for signal-processing innovations will survive § 101 scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court invalidated them on indefiniteness grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of invalidity but on alternative grounds, holding that while the district court erred in finding the claims indefinite, the claims were invalid for lack of enablement. The court found that the patent's specification did not enable the full scope of the claimed invention—transmitting signals over air using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match impedance—because accomplishing impedance matching as broadly claimed would require undue experimentation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative enablement grounds even when the district court's primary indefiniteness rationale was incorrect, providing multiple defensive pathways against broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that appellate courts may independently identify enablement deficiencies not raised below, and broadly drafted claims covering fundamental physical principles may be particularly vulnerable to enablement challenges.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient reasoning when denying a motion for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 post-Alice and abandoned.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of Pen-Tech's motion for Rule 11 sanctions and § 285 attorney fees, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The court noted significant indicators that Epic Tech's infringement claims may have been objectively baseless, including PTO § 101 rejections of related applications post-Alice that Epic Tech abandoned without overcoming.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers who prevail on § 101 grounds gain stronger tools to recover attorney fees and sanctions when patent holders press claims despite clear signals of invalidity, potentially deterring frivolous patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened fee-shifting risk when asserting patents whose related applications were rejected under § 101, particularly if they cannot articulate meaningful distinctions between the asserted and rejected claims.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification discloses preparation methods and characterization data for the claimed crystalline forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description for claims covering crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate, the active ingredient in the cancer drug Cabometyx®. The decision upholds key patent protection for Exelixis's blockbuster oncology product through 2030, rejecting MSN's challenge that the specification failed to adequately describe the claimed crystalline salt forms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from the affirmation that specifications disclosing preparation methods and characterization data for crystalline drug forms satisfy written description, strengthening protection for branded drugs against generic challengers in Hatch-Waxman litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products and similar drugs protected by crystalline form patents, potentially delaying lower-cost alternatives for cancer patients.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the term 'internal diameter' in a patent claim for an oil and gas wellbore float tool refers only to the measured width across the pipe or can also refer to a diameter along the length of the pipe.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment of infringement and damages award in a patent case involving oil and gas wellbore casing technology, remanding for further proceedings based on claim construction of the term 'internal diameter.' The case involves NCS's patent on float tools using rupture discs for casing flotation in horizontal wells, with the construction of this key term determining whether Nine Energy's competing BreakThru product infringes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment industry benefit from the Federal Circuit's close scrutiny of claim terms, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims and providing opportunities to design around patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy equipment sector face uncertainty when key claim terms have multiple plausible constructions, as remand for new proceedings increases litigation costs and delays enforcement of patent rights.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in a single order, rather than dismissing solely on venue grounds and transferring the case.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both venue and § 101 eligibility grounds, holding that after finding venue improper, the court did not err by also reaching the merits of patent eligibility. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was held ineligible under § 101. The court rejected AML's argument that the district court should have stopped at the venue ruling.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals (such as § 101 ineligibility) even when venue is also improper, providing a more definitive resolution that prevents the patent holder from simply re-filing in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent holders lose the ability to avoid merits rulings by arguing that improper venue should be the sole basis for dismissal, increasing the risk of adverse precedent on patent eligibility when filing in strategically chosen but improper venues.
